memoryText: Rend your hearts and not your garments. Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love; and he relents over disaster.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Joel 2:13 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is a call to real repentance, and it begins with a contrast. It does not say that outward signs are wrong. It says they are not enough.

“Rend your hearts and not your garments.” In the ancient world, tearing your clothes was the standard sign of grief or repentance. But a person could tear a garment and keep a hard heart. God asks for the real thing. Sorrow over sin, turning from it, wanting God. In Psalm 51:17, David says, “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit.”

“Return to the LORD your God.” The call is to return, to come home. The picture is of someone who has wandered and needs to return to a loving master. “Your God.” Even in rebellion, he is still their God.

“For he is gracious and merciful.” This is the reason to return. It is not that you can earn his favor, but that he is already kind. Gracious means he gives what we do not deserve. Merciful means he does not give what we do deserve.

“Slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love.” His anger is real but slow. His love is abundant, overflowing. This is God’s own description of himself in Exodus 34:6, and it is repeated across the Old Testament, in Nehemiah 9:17, Psalm 145:8, Jonah 4:2, and here.

“And he relents over disaster.” God is willing to turn back from judgment when people turn to him. This does not mean God changes his character, but that he responds to repentance with mercy.

Whenever you feel you have failed, say this verse. It describes a God who is waiting.
weekInReview: This week you finished the Chronicler’s story of the fall of Judah, with Manasseh’s repentance in Babylon and Josiah’s finding of the Book of the Law. You saw how the book ends with an open door: “Let him go up.” Then you moved to the prophets of the return. In Joel, a swarm of locusts became a picture of the coming day of the LORD, and the prophet’s call was clear: “Return to me with all your heart.” You read the promise of the Spirit poured out on all flesh, and a fountain from the house of the LORD. In Obadiah, you heard God judge proud Edom for standing aloof in the day of Judah’s trouble, and promise that the kingdom shall be the LORD’s. In Psalms 97 and 98, you sang that the LORD reigns and that all the ends of the earth will see his salvation.
reflectionQuestions: Joel says to rend your heart and not your garments. What outward religious habits in your life need an inner reality behind them?
Obadiah condemns standing aloof when a brother suffers. Whom in your life might you be tempted to ignore?
Joel promised the Spirit on all flesh, and Peter said it came at Pentecost. How have you seen the Spirit at work in your life or in your church?
prayerPrompts: Return to God with all your heart.
Thank him for pouring out his Spirit.
